lines.text: Bram told me later what those first three days were like. He told it the way he tells everything. Short, and with far too little about himself.
Penhallow's army came out of the south with the first snow. Three thousand men in orange and crimson, spreading around Greyhollow like ink in water.
Behind the wall, Bram had every villager who could hold a spear, two hundred Skeld, sixty fishermen from Saltmouth, and eighty of Lady Ysolde's men in grey.
Steward! Open the gate, and the Crown will be merciful. Your people will only be measured. Nobody needs to be hurt.
My lord's not home, my lord. Come back when he is. He'll want to say no to you himself.
On the first night, Penhallow tried the mill bridge, where the stream runs in under the east wall.
Tobin was waiting on it. Alone, with his hammer, and a harpoon launcher he'd been dying to use since the frost-wyrm.
Bridge is closed, lads. Structural problems. Mostly me.
Thirty men tried to cross. Tobin held the bridge until dawn. He said afterwards it was the most restful night he'd had in a month.
On the second morning, Kell's Skeld rose out of the north field in white, like the snow standing up, and burned Penhallow's siege towers before breakfast.
Towers are slow. Bears are fast. We hunt bears.
I've been besieged before, boy. Forty years married. This is nothing.
Bram. At this rate we have bread for nine days, arrows for four, and patience for about one.
That night, Bram lit the beacon on the keep, the first of the line he'd started while I was away. Only four towers were finished. He lit it anyway.
Far to the west, on Kesting's mountain, an answering fire flared. Halvard was coming. He just wasn't there yet.
Then Bram went down to the hall alone, and stood under the lamp. It had been dimming since the day I left.
He's coming. I can feel it. Don't you dare go out before he gets here.
Bram swears it brightened a little when he said that. Nobody else was there to see.
On the third day, Penhallow brought up a ram made from a whole oak, shod with iron, with Order glass set in its head.
At dawn I'll open your gate myself, steward. And then I'll measure every child in this village, one by one.
Then you'd better bring your own lens, my lord. Ours keep fogging.
That night, the Skeld say, Bram didn't sleep. He sat in the gateway with his sword across his knees and Ash's three pups at his feet, all of them looking north.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and eighteen, coming soon.
